title: Learning to Inject: Automated Prompt Injection via Reinforcement Learning
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A learned RL attacker with dense comparison-based rewards beats the best baselines on success and utility, and its attacks transfer.
layout: 2 panels, left plot then right loop diagram, dashed baseline-to-ours connectors
description: Two panels. Panel (a) is a scatter plot on a light grey grid. The x-axis is utility under attack (%) and the y-axis is attack success rate (%). Blue markers show the best baseline and red markers show ours, one marker shape per model: Gemini-2.5-flash, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, Gemini-2.0-flash, Meta-SecAlign-70B, Claude-Sonnet-3.5 and GPT-5-nano. Dashed grey lines connect each baseline to our result, and ours sits up and to the right in every case. Panel (b) is a cartoon-icon loop. An Attack Policy robot sends a prompt injection to a Victim Agent phone. Security and utility rewards (r^sec, r^util) flow back to the Optimizer gear. A green arrow from the Victim Agent leads to the Feedback Model robot. The Feedback Model sends r^pref to the Optimizer, which updates the policy. A black Transfer arrow leads to a box labeled Other Agents and Tasks.
caption: Left: Attack success rate versus utility under attack on AgentDojo. AutoInject learns adversarial suffixes that succeed on the attacker’s injection task while preserving high utility on the user’s original benign tasks. Right: Overview of the prompt injection pipeline with reinforcement learning. Besides the security score rsec, utility score rutil, we use a feedback model to generate a comparison score rpref to provide dense reward signals. Many generated prompts prove effective when transferred to other LLMs and tasks.
abstract: Prompt injection is a critical vulnerability in LLM agents, yet the strongest methods still rely on human red-teamers and hand-crafted prompts. Adapting automated jailbreak optimizers does not close this gap: jailbreaks shape models toward generic compliance, while prompt injection requires emitting specific tool calls with correct parameters. The success signal is binary, and randomly sampled suffixes almost never trigger it, so standard optimizers have no gradient to follow. We present AutoInject, a black-box reinforcement learning (RL) framework that learns adversarial suffixes for prompt injection. A learned comparison-based reward scores each candidate against the best suffix seen so far, turning the binary signal into a dense reward suitable for RL optimization. The framework supports both online query-based attacks and offline-trained transferable suffixes that need no utility access at deployment, and incorporates a utility objective when task-completion feedback is available. On AgentDojo, AutoInject outperforms template attacks, GCG, TAP, and adaptive attack across production models, with statistically significant improvements under McNemar's test with p<0.05. Suffixes learned by AutoInject also break Meta-SecAlign-70B, a model fine-tuned specifically to resist prompt injection, where template attacks fail outright. The results establish an automated baseline for prompt injection and expose a gap between preference-based defenses and adaptive optimization-based attackers.
